newsitem.title: USA: Dial to cut 250 jobs, 20 percent in overhead cost.
newsitem.headline: Dial to cut 250 jobs, 20 percent in overhead cost.

text.p: Dial Corp., maker of Dial soaps, Purex detergents and Brillo scouring pads, said Wednesday it plans to cut about 250 jobs and sell or discontinue some of its brands, for an annual pretax savings of about $40 million.
The Phoenix, Ariz.-based company said it expects to take a one-time writeoff of about $50 million in the third quarter to cover all costs associated with the changes.

It said it expects its 1996 earnings will be about 15 percent lower than the consensus of analysts' forecasts of 85 cents a share, due to "slowness in new-product acceptance," as well as selected detergent and personal care programmes.
As part of the changes, the company said it plans to reduce its overhead costs by 20 percent.

Of the 250 job cuts, about 80 percent are to come from management and administration, it said. That would leave Dial with about 2,800 employees, a 33 percent drop from 4,200 in 1990. Dial said it would notify affected employees Wednesday.

Dial was separated from its travel services division, now called Viad Corp., in a spin-off in August 1995. Before that, Dial closed six of its U.S. manufacturing plants and cut nearly 700 jobs, mainly at the production plants. Management and corporate staff positions were virtually untouched during the cutback.

Dial said about half of the pretax savings will be used to improve short-term earnings per share, while the rest will be used to improve its long-term profitability through investments in brand equity and technology improvements.
"We are realists," said Malcolm Jozoff, Dial's chairman, president and chief executive, in a statement.

"If a company our size doesn't take the difficult steps necessary to achieve profitable growth, some bigger company just might come along and show us how to do it. We know what we have to do, and we are doing it."
Dial, which also makes Armour Star food products and Renuzit air fresheners, did not identify the products it intends to discontinue or sell.

Dial said it plans to move from its present headquarters in a Phoenix office tower that it shares with its former parent company because the space is too large and costly for the streamlined company. The company is considering several metropolitan areas, including Phoenix, and expects to reach a decision by year end.
Dial's stock was up 12.5 cents to $13.125 on the New York Stock Exchange.
